Partially filled from England's published itemization of the condemned propositions; the verification flag stays until the original printing is read.

title: Brigham Young on the succession of Gods — and his caution
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:333)

quotes.excerpt: How many Gods there are, I do not know. But there never was a time when there were not Gods and worlds, and when men were not passing through the same ordeals that we are now passing through. That course has been from all eternity, and it is and will be to all eternity.
quotes.note: Succession of Gods, not merely plurality of worlds — this is what the tightened INFINITE-CHAIN tag requires.

notes: Hearsay raised from E to C in v2. Most Journal of Discourses material derives from George Watt's contemporaneous shorthand, edited for publication and in the early years reviewed by Young's office — that is contemporaneous secondhand with an editing layer, not untraceable attribution. E is now reserved for genuinely orphaned attributions. The pairing is what makes this entry valuable: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest official discouragement of the question. Quote verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses 7:333 (page-scan collation). The “origin of the Gods” caution formerly held here as a placeholder belongs to a different discourse — see young-origin-caution-1859, delivered the next day of the same conference.

title: B. H. Roberts: an endless line of Gods stretching back into the eternities
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: A New Witness for God (Salt Lake City: George Q. Cannon & Sons, 1895), ch. XXX, p. 466

witnesses.scribe: Mormon Texts Project transcription of the 1895 first edition
witnesses.note: Independent full-text transcription; collated against the page scan and agrees word for word.

quotes.excerpt: But if God the Father was not always God, but came to his present exalted position by degrees of progress as indicated in the teachings of the prophet, how has there been a God from all eternity? The answer is that there has been and there now exists an endless line of Gods, stretching back into the eternities, that had no beginning and will have no end. Their existence runs parallel with endless duration, and their dominions are as limitless as boundless space.
quotes.note: The most explicit published chain statement by a General Authority in the nineteenth century, and note its logical role: Roberts offers the endless line as the solution to a problem the King Follett Discourse creates. If God was once a man, how has there been a God from all eternity? Because there has always been another one behind him. The regress here is a piece of apologetic repair work, not an independent revelation claim.

quotes.excerpt: D'ye think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be?
quotes.note: Roberts prints W. W. Phelps's “If You Could Hie to Kolob” in full immediately after the prose statement, as the hymnodic form of the same claim. This is why the chain outlives the prose that carries it: the hymn stayed in the hymnbook long after General Authorities stopped writing sentences like the one above.

notes: Verified verbatim twice over against the 1895 first edition: the Internet Archive page scan (printed p. 466) and the Mormon Texts Project's independent transcription. Chapter XXX is titled “Evidence of Divine Inspiration in Joseph Smith Derived from the Prophet's Teaching in Regard to the Extent of the Universe, Man's Place in It and His Doctrine Respecting the Gods—Concluded”; the passage sits directly after Roberts's block quotation of the King Follett Discourse (see kfd-1844), which is what raises the question the endless line answers. Graded never-official: Roberts sat in the First Council of the Seventy and the book was issued by the church-affiliated George Q. Cannon & Sons, but it carried no First Presidency commission — unlike Talmage's Articles of Faith four years later — and it functioned as a missionary apologetic rather than as a doctrinal standard.

title: James E. Talmage: a God who is Himself progressive
speaker: James E. Talmage
office: Author writing under commission of the First Presidency (ordained an Apostle 1911)
venue: The Articles of Faith, Lecture XXIV, “Practical Religion” (p. 430 in early printings)

quotes.excerpt: We believe in a God who is Himself progressive, whose majesty is intelligence; whose perfection consists in eternal advancement; the perpetual work of whose creation stands “finished, yet renewed forever;”—a Being who has attained His exalted state by a path which now His children are permitted to follow; whose glory it is their heritage to share.
quotes.note: Affirmation — the canonical statement of ongoing divine progression in an officially commissioned doctrinal work. Contrast Talmage in the April 1915 Conference Report (“was once a Man, and has progressed … to His present position”), which is completed past progression, not this claim — the same apostle, sixteen years apart, saying two different things that sound identical.

quotes.excerpt: In spite of the opposition of all the sects, in the face of direct charges of blasphemy, the Church proclaims the eternal truth, “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.”
quotes.note: The Snow couplet proclaimed as “eternal truth” against blasphemy charges — a useful register datum for 1899 confidence, three sentences after the progression claim.

notes: Text verified against the printed lecture. The book was prepared and published under First Presidency commission and served as a semi-official doctrinal standard for decades; it is not current curriculum.

title: Nels L. Nelson: how our Father became God
speaker: Nels L. Nelson
office: Professor of English, Brigham Young University
venue: Scientific Aspects of Mormonism; or, Religion in Terms of Life (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1904), ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God,” pp. 273–276

quotes.excerpt: As respects the eternal principles underlying His purposes, He never changes; these form the very warp and woof of His divine perfection; but as respects the methods or devices for bringing about these purposes, He changes as the exigency requires; and the variations possible to His invention are practically infinite… It is by reason of this very principle of mutation in God that we perceive all things to be in a state of evolution here on earth.
quotes.note: Affirmation — but a bounded one, and the boundary has to be quoted with it. Nelson's God changes in method, not in principle, and the sentences just above hold that on attaining Godhood “how could He be other than immutable? For change would then imply degeneracy.” Lifting “this very principle of mutation in God” out of that setting produces a stronger divine-progression claim than Nelson makes.

quotes.excerpt: But since by this conception He is made to belong to the same order of beings as Christ, His Son,—the same order, indeed, as man himself,—and must consequently have attained to Godhood or creative power, it becomes a pertinent question to consider how He reached such divine sovereignty.
quotes.note: The chapter's opening question, carried as context because it is routinely quoted as though it were the chapter's answer. Note the original begins “But since by this conception…” — the concessive “But” is part of the sentence and is preserved here.

quotes.excerpt: A sufficient general answer, therefore, would be that God became God because He fulfilled the law of becoming perfect as His Father in heaven was perfect; or, in the terms of science, because He fulfilled the supreme requirements of psychic evolution.
quotes.note: Explicit divine parentage — “His Father in heaven,” a phrase Nelson builds by turning Matthew 5:48 back on God himself — with no chain length stated and no interest in stating one. The gloss “psychic evolution” is the Spencerian idiom that marks this whole cluster of Utah writers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the 1904 Putnam's first edition (item scientificaspect00nelsrich), reading continuously from printed p. 273 through p. 276 so the page breaks between the three quotes are known rather than assumed: the divine-progression material closes ch. XXV at pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God” opens at p. 275 with the question and answers it on pp. 275–276. Nelson was a BYU English professor writing for a national trade press, not for the Church; never-official. He is one of the few authors in the dataset who is both a backward-explicit source and a divine-progression source, which is precisely why his two claims should not be merged into one: the parentage is asserted, the ongoing mutability is heavily qualified, and neither entails the other.

title: B. H. Roberts, The Seventy's Course in Theology
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: President of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: Seventy's Course in Theology (five volumes); later The Truth, The Way, The Life

quotes.excerpt: [Roberts's articulation of intelligence → spirit → body: an eternal, uncreated intelligence is at some point organized into a spirit body by Heavenly Parents, and later receives a physical body. Exact excerpt to be pulled from the Course in Theology volumes.]
quotes.note: Placeholder excerpt; the framework needs quoting directly from Roberts rather than paraphrased.

notes: Added in v2 as the actual origin of the three-stage model, which v1 wrongly retrojected onto Abraham 3. Roberts's synthesis is what harmonizes Abraham 3's eternalism with 1909-era viviparism: it lets spirits be literally begotten while their underlying intelligence remains uncreated. Never official, but it became the default framework in twentieth-century teaching. Link out to bhroberts.org for the primary volumes.

title: Orson F. Whitney: a Mother in heaven defended as philosophy
speaker: Orson F. Whitney
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1907)

quotes.excerpt: Why, then, should it be deemed unphilosophic for man, the child of God, — man and woman, male and female, — to become like their Father and their Mother in heaven? We are at the defiance of the world to prove this doctrine unphilosophical.
quotes.note: A Mother in heaven asserted in passing and then used as a premise, which is the tell: Whitney does not argue for her, he assumes her and dares the world to refute the package. Tagged HEAVENLY-MOTHER only. “Become like their Father and their Mother in heaven” is theosis, not generative exaltation, and carries no FORWARD tag by itself — the A-framing trap. Spacing before the question mark normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed.

quotes.excerpt: You earthly parents expect your children to become men and women like yourselves. You know that it is only a question of time, when, if they live, your little toddling children will become men and women, and will marry and have children of their own.
quotes.note: Marked implied. The sentence is literally about mortal children. But it is the immediate warrant for the claim in q1 — the analogy is offered so that the hearer will complete it — and what completes it is offspring, not merely likeness. Whitney stops one step short of saying so, so the forward-generative reading is carried as read-into rather than stated.

quotes.excerpt: It revealed anew the sublime fact that man is verily the child of Deity, and can become, by development, like unto his Father and his God. It taught the great truth that man is divinity in embryo, and capable, by education, through human experience, and by obedience to the principles of eternal progress, of rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father, who desires to make His children equal with Himself, and to put into their possession all things.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. “Divinity in embryo,” “equal with Himself,” “rising to the plane whereon stands the Universal Father” — this is theosis at full nineteenth-century strength and it still asserts nothing about spirit offspring or about a chain behind the Father. Recorded so the entry shows what Whitney does and does not claim in the same breath.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1907/1907-10-whitney-defending-the-saints.md, whose Final Review collated the full body against the archive.org scan conferencereport1907sa, leaves n45–n53, word for word against the printed page. A heavyweight pass had earlier split a separate George F. Richards address out of this file and re-anchored the leaf, so the URL points at where Whitney's own remarks begin. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. No hymn quotation appears in this talk, which is why the entry carries no citesId — Whitney reaches the Mother without Eliza R. Snow, through the same argument from nature that Erastus Snow used in 1885 (see snow-heavenly-mother-1885), but stripped of the anatomy and recast as a reply to outside critics. The setting matters: the talk is an apologetic defense of the Saints “against calumny and misrepresentation,” and the Heavenly Mother claim is deployed as an asset rather than defended as an embarrassment. Read against packer-parentage-1984 and hinckley-1997, which handle the same apologetic pressure by subtraction.

title: Heber C. Iverson: the hymn credited to Joseph Smith's inspiration
speaker: Heber C. Iverson
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon overflow session (Conference Report, April 1908, pp. 69–72)

quotes.excerpt: In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: The couplet as printed in the Conference Report; Iverson quotes the first three stanzas and stops here. Spacing before the question mark, semicolon and exclamation point normalized from the printed OCR; no words changed. See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: That doctrine was ridiculed seventy years ago, when announced by this hymn, teaching what had been given by inspiration flowing first through the mind of the Prophet Joseph Smith, that we have a mother in heaven.
quotes.note: The provenance claim that the whole later tradition rests on, made explicit from the pulpit: the hymn is not Eliza R. Snow's poetic inference but a vehicle for revelation given first to Joseph Smith. Set this beside snow-heavenly-mother-1885, where an apostle says the opposite in as many words — “it is left for us to infer this” — and beside hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991, where the argument has shrunk to the observation that Joseph made no correction to what Sister Snow had written. The date arithmetic is loose: “seventy years ago” from 1908 lands in 1838, while the poem was published in 1845.

quotes.excerpt: He discourses very learnedly upon the dual sequence of the term Elohim, and proves conclusively by his deduction that there is a feminine element existing with the Deity, and that we have in Deity a mother as well as a father. There are mothers of our spirits.
quotes.note: Two things worth having. First, the corroboration is outside and secular — an unnamed writer in “one of the leading magazines of this country” arguing from the plural form of Elohim — which is a Latter-day Saint apostle-era bishop reaching for a non-Mormon philologist to underwrite a Mormon doctrine. Second, and easy to miss, the plural: “There are mothers of our spirits.” Iverson slides from one Mother to many without remark, twenty years after the Manifesto and in a Church still living with plural marriage, and the plural never becomes a doctrine anyone defends.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1908/1908-04-iverson-rejoicing-and-responsibility.md, whose heavyweight pass verified the talk boundary, speaker, session and supplied title against the archive.org Conference Report scan conferencereport1908a at printed pages 69–72, and whose Final Review pass is recorded as complete. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId preserving the edge to o-my-father: the hymn is quoted at length, but the entry's value is the three claims Iverson builds around it — that the doctrine came by inspiration through Joseph Smith, that a secular philologist independently confirms it, and that our spirits have mothers plural — none of which is in the hymn. He is a ward bishop speaking in an overflow session, so this is not authoritative teaching; it is evidence of what a well-read local leader took the hymn to have settled, which for the reception history is the more useful thing.

title: First Presidency, “The Origin of Man”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith, John R. Winder, Anthon H. Lund
venue: Improvement Era (official statement)

quotes.excerpt: All men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother, and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity... man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father, prior to coming upon the earth in a temporal body.
quotes.note: The strongest viviparous statement in the corpus, and the only one that says both begotten and born.

quotes.excerpt: [Man is] the offspring of celestial parentage... capable, by experience through ages and aeons, of evolving into a God.
quotes.note: Tagged BACKWARD-MORTALITY per the v2 revision, but flagging a tension for review: as excerpted, the sentence runs forward (man evolving into a God), not backward (God having been man). It reads as a First Presidency forward-progression claim — arguably FORWARD-EUPHEMISM, since no mechanism is named — and only yields a backward claim by running the couplet's inference in reverse. Confirm the exact wording against the 1909 Improvement Era text, then settle the tag. Retag resolved: with BACKWARD-MORTALITY retired, this moves to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than onto the Father axis. The sentence runs forward — man evolving into a God, no mechanism named — and never claims the Father was mortal. Confirm the Improvement Era wording; if it does contain a backward clause, move it to FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE.

notes: Verify quote 2's wording before relying on it; if confirmed it makes 1909 a stronger forward-progression statement than it is usually remembered as being. The February 2002 Ensign reprint is filed separately as a citation — its timing, five years after the Hinckley interviews, is the datum.

title: B. H. Roberts: God's immutability does not exclude advancement or progress of God
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: President of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: The Seventy's Course in Theology, Fourth Year: The Atonement (Salt Lake City: The Deseret News, 1911), 69–70

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression: Two Complementary Ways to Talk About God,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 43, citing The Seventy's Course in Theology (Deseret News Press, 1911), 69–70
witnesses.note: England's catalogue entry, which is what led here; his reproduction is lowercase OCR and drops the “so” from “should not be so understood.” The excerpts below are from the Roberts volume, not from England.

quotes.excerpt: But God's immutability should not be so understood as to exclude the idea of advancement or progress of God. Thus, for example: God's kingdom and glory may be enlarged, as more and more redeemed souls are added to his kingdom… So that in this sense there may come change and progress even for God.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and the ground it stands on matters: Roberts derives divine progress from the enlargement of God's kingdom and glory — the very same “dominions, not knowledge” move that Bruce R. McConkie would later use to *deny* progression (see mcconkie-heresies-1980 and millet-mcconkie-life-beyond-1986). The difference is that Roberts does not stop there; see the next quote. Elision marks a phrase carrying scan artifacts in the digitized page.

quotes.excerpt: an absolute immutability would require eternal immobility—which would reduce God to a condition eternally static, which, from the nature of things, would bar him from participation in that enlargement of kingdom and increasing glory that comes from redemption and the progress of men.
quotes.note: The argument stated negatively: an unqualified immutability is not reverence but paralysis. The same stagnation-is-death reasoning runs through Hugh B. Brown's April 1956 conference address (see brown-deify-man-1956), where it has been transferred from God to man.

quotes.excerpt: So with the All-knowing attribute, Omniscience: that must be understood somewhat in the same light as the other attributes considered: not that God is Omniscient up to the point that further progress in knowledge is impossible to him; but that all knowledge that is, all that exists, God knows.
quotes.note: The sharper half of the claim, and the one England does not quote: Roberts takes progression into knowledge, not merely dominion. This is the precise proposition Joseph Fielding Smith calls “very dangerous” forty-three years later (jfsmith-doctrines-salvation-1954) and McConkie calls a deadly heresy in 1980, and it is here in a Church-published quorum study course written by the President of the First Council of the Seventy.

notes: Verified by pulling the printed pages themselves from the Gospel Scholar Archive copy of the collected Seventy's Course in Theology (PDF pp. 802–804 = printed pp. 68–70 of Year Book IV), and confirming from the volume's own title page (PDF p. 727) that the 1911 Deseret News imprint England cites is Fourth Year: The Atonement. Line-break hyphenation has been closed up; one phrase carrying scan damage is elided. The passage sits in a numbered section headed “7. Limitation in the Attributes of God,” immediately after Roberts's treatments of Omnipotence, Omniscience and Omnipresence, and is footnoted to a long quotation from Sir Oliver Lodge — the philosophical provenance England and Matthew Bowman both trace to Herbert Spencer-era British thought. correlationStatus is graded historical-official here because the Year Books were prepared by Roberts in his office as President of the First Council of the Seventy, issued by the Church's own press, and used as the prescribed course of study for Seventies quorums; note that the existing bh-roberts-tripartite entry grades the same series never-official, and the two should be reconciled by the maintainer rather than left divergent. This entry is deliberately *not* the tripartite-framework entry: bh-roberts-tripartite covers intelligence → spirit → body and still needs its own excerpt pulled from the Year Books; this one covers only the progression claim.

title: Charles W. Penrose: the gift of endless, perpetual increase
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 48–54)

quotes.excerpt: One of the grand things referred to by President Smith as in the revelations of God to the Prophet Joseph, was the eternity of the marriage covenant, by which the man and the woman may be joined together according to God's order, and though death may part them, yet in the resurrection they shall come forth to be husband and wife, to be parents of children, to have the gift of endless, perpetual increase, the beginning of their kingdom and their glory in worlds without end. That is real life, the power to continue and the power to produce and to increase, the power of vitality in the spirit and in the body.
quotes.note: Explicit rather than euphemistic: resurrected couples are named as “parents of children,” and the increase is qualified twice over as endless and perpetual. “Worlds without end” here is the liturgical idiom for eternity, not a claim about plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is not applied. The Conference Report OCR prints “bv President Smith”; corrected to “by,” a scan artifact, with no other change to the wording.

quotes.excerpt: And those who follow in the footsteps of Jesus Christ, who is now to all purposes like the Father, will inherit similar glory, and it will never fade away, and it will be exemplified in them to the full. The spirit of life will be within them in body and in spirit, and they will increase forever and ever, and like the blessing that comes to our elder brother, Jesus Christ, of the increase of their kingdom there shall be no end.
quotes.note: The forward chain closed against Christ's own case: the exalted inherit what the Son inherited, and the increase of their kingdom is unending. The vault transcription prints a stray period in “elder .brother,” an OCR artifact of the printed column; removed here, wording otherwise untouched.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-15-charles-w-penrose-remarks-15.md. Conference Report, so A. That file has an unusually heavy repair history — two long passages were scrambled by two-column OCR and were later de-interleaved directly against the archive.org page images (leaves n48–n56, printed pp. 48–54) — but neither quoted passage falls inside the repaired blocks, and both read cleanly apart from the two isolated scan artifacts noted on the quotes. Two corrections to how this source is usually described. First the date: the pulpit report gives 6 October, but the vault frontmatter and the printed session heading place it in the second day afternoon session, 7 October 1911. Second the office: he is frequently cited as First Presidency here, but Penrose was not called as a counselor until December 1911, so in October he was still of the Twelve. Why it matters: this is post-Manifesto, official, and undiminished. Twenty-one years after plural marriage ended, the full generative package is preached in general conference without hedging — which is the evidence that the early twentieth century softened the vocabulary of deification, not the doctrine of increase.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “a few ignoramuses, ‘learned fools’” who limit God to the capacity of man
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
venue: General conference opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, April 1914)

quotes.excerpt: It is true that we have, now and then, here and there, occasionally, persons who would, if they possibly could, limit the power, the knowledge, the wisdom of God Almighty, to the capacity of men. We have a few of them among us, and some of them have been, and may be, school teachers.
quotes.note: Denial, and the one detail that fixes its target: “school teachers.” This is 1914, three years after the Brigham Young University modernism dismissals, and the finite-God, God-still-learning position was being taught by Church educators — compare nelson-scientific-aspects-1904, written by a BYU professor. The claim being rejected is that God's knowledge and power are bounded by what man can conceive.

quotes.excerpt: I say again that there are just a few ignoramuses, “learned fools,” if you please, who would make you believe, if they could, that Almighty God is limited in His power to the capacity of man. Don't you believe it, not for one moment.
quotes.note: Denial, in the register the phrase is famous for. Read the intervening text before using it as a straight progression datum: the specific charges Smith enumerates are that the miracles were “mere symbols,” that Christ could not turn water into wine or walk on water, and that the Father and Son did not appear to Joseph Smith in person. The proposition on the page is a denial of miracle and of divine omnipotence, not the technical claim that God is still acquiring knowledge; “the knowledge, the wisdom” of the previous quote is the only part that reaches the progression question directly.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1914/1914-04-00-smith-opening-address.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1914a, leaves n2–n10) and Final-Reviewed against an independent column-order reconstruction of the same scan. Conference Report, so A. The talk was missing from the vault's original ingest and was recovered whole in a later pass, which is why it does not appear in earlier sweeps of the 1914 conference. Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 40, files this under the deniers of divine progression alongside Joseph Fielding Smith; the excerpt is taken from the Conference Report rather than from England's lowercase OCR rendering, and the note above records where England's framing runs ahead of what the printed text says. The pairing that makes the entry worth having is chronological: Roberts publishes the progression claim in a Church-issued priesthood course in 1911, and the President of the Church calls its holders learned fools from the pulpit in 1914.

title: John A. Widtsoe: a progressive God, and Many Gods who are peers rather than ancestors
speaker: John A. Widtsoe
office: President of the Agricultural College of Utah (ordained an Apostle 1921)
venue: Rational Theology As Taught by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (General Priesthood Committee, 1915), ch. 6 “God and Man,” pp. 23–25

quotes.excerpt: However, if the great law of progression is accepted, God must have been engaged from the beginning, and must now be engaged in progressive development, and, infinite as God is, he must have been less powerful in the past than he is today. While it is folly for man to attempt to unravel in detail the mystery of the past, yet it is only logical to believe that a progressive God has not always possessed his present position.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and an unusually unhedged one — “must now be engaged in progressive development,” present tense. This is the claim Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie later call dangerous and heretical.

quotes.excerpt: We may be certain that, through self-effort, the inherent and innate powers of God have been developed to a God-like degree. Thus, he has become God… His Godhood, however, was attained by the use of his power in simple obedience to the laws he discovered as he grew in experience.
quotes.note: Untagged deliberately. This is completed past attainment, not past mortality and not parentage: Widtsoe's God rose from among co-existing intelligences by self-effort, and no Father of God appears anywhere in the chapter. Tagging it backward-mortality would import the King Follett frame Widtsoe is quietly declining to use.

quotes.excerpt: Next to God, there may be, therefore, other intelligent beings so nearly approaching his power as to be coequal with him in all things so far as our finite understanding can perceive… Under this definition there may be a great number of intelligent beings who possess to a greater or less degree the quality of Godhood.
quotes.note: The section is headed “Many Gods,” and this is the sentence that gets recruited as regress evidence. It is the opposite: Widtsoe's Many Gods are contemporaries thrown up by parallel progression from a common field of intelligences — peers, near-equals, “coequal with him” — not a line of ancestors. Nothing in the chapter stands behind God.

quotes.excerpt: Man is, nevertheless, moving on, in eternal progression. “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” In short, man is a god in embryo. He comes of a race of gods, and as his eternal growth is continued, he will approach more nearly the point which to us is Godhood.
quotes.note: The Snow couplet is the only backward-mortality content in the chapter, and Widtsoe imports it as a summary rather than deriving it. “He comes of a race of gods” is about man's ancestry, not God's.

notes: Verified verbatim against a scan of the 1915 first edition, whose title page reads “Published for the Use of the Melchizedek Priesthood by the General Priesthood Committee, 1915” — hence historical-official rather than never-official, though the book was never canonical and is long out of print. Printed pp. 23–25 in that edition carry chapter 6, matching the pagination Eugene England uses. Watch the edition when quoting: the Paulsen and Fisher review in FARMS Review 15/2 quotes the 1965 Deseret Book printing, which reads “if the law of progression be accepted” where the 1915 text collated here reads “if the great law of progression is accepted,” and the surrounding sentences differ likewise. Recorded as a divine-progression affirmation and emphatically not as a chain source: this is the taxonomy's fourth trap in its purest form, a source that affirms ongoing divine progression while asserting no divine ancestry at all. Structurally it belongs with Penrose (1884) and Nelson (1904).

title: James E. Talmage: the Eternal Father was once a Man, by right of conquest
speaker: James E. Talmage
venue: General conference, third day morning session (Conference Report, April 1915, p. 123)

quotes.excerpt: you can't change the fact that He is the Son of that Father, and that Father, the Eternal Father, the Father of Jesus Christ, the Father of His spirit and the Father of His body, was once a Man, and has progressed, not by any favor but by the right of conquest over sin, and over death, to His present position of priesthood and power, of Godship and Godliness, as the Supreme Being whom we all profess to worship.
quotes.note: BACKWARD-MORTALITY, and emphatically not DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Every verb is completed: was once a Man, has progressed, to His present position. The progression is a finished ascent that terminates in Godship, not an ongoing increase — Talmage is here answering the question of how the Father came to be God, not whether He is still growing. The referent is unmistakable and unusually over-specified: he names the Eternal Father four ways in one clause, so this cannot be read Christologically the way the Snow couplet can. “Right of conquest” is the distinctive contribution: exaltation earned rather than conferred.

quotes.excerpt: It was crystallized into what we may call an aphorism, by President Lorenzo Snow: "As man is God once was; as God is man may be". We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man. In the sense in which Christ was perfect in His sphere, we may become perfect in ours.
quotes.note: The couplet, and immediately a Christological gloss on it — “We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man” — which is exactly the ambiguity catalogued at snow-couplet. Referent ambiguous for this quote even though the entry's referent is the Father, because Talmage's own next sentence supplies the Son as the illustration. Note also the demotion in status: the couplet is “what we may call an aphorism,” not revelation. Spacing around the semicolons in the vault transcription reflects OCR of the printed Report and has been normalized; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-34-james-e-talmage-remarks-34.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report and verified against a word-coordinate reading-order reconstruction of the archive.org DjVu OCR (conferencereport1915a, leaf anchor n121); the Final Review pass found no body change needed. Conference Report, so A. The office is given as the generic “General Authority” in the vault frontmatter; Talmage had been ordained an Apostle in December 1911 and was of the Twelve in April 1915. This entry exists chiefly to be read against talmage-af-1899, and the pairing is the point: the same author, sixteen years apart, makes two claims that sound identical and are not. In 1899 he wrote of “a God who is Himself progressive… whose perfection consists in eternal advancement” — present tense, ongoing, DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Here in 1915 he says the Father “was once a Man, and has progressed… to His present position” — past tense, completed, BACKWARD-MORTALITY. Conflating the two is trap #1 running in the opposite direction from usual, and it is how a single author gets cited on both sides of the twentieth-century progression debate.

title: Rudger Clawson: “Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?”
speaker: Rudger Clawson
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (Conference Report, October 1929)

quotes.excerpt: We understand, from the scriptures, that Jesus Christ is our elder brother. If that be the case then we are his younger brothers and younger sisters; we belonged to a great family before we came into the world. It was the family of God, for Jesus said: "When you pray, say our Father which art in heaven. Our Father is there, and we believe that we have a mother there. That thought was beautifully expressed in the hymn that the choir sang this morning. I think you will agree with me that it is a very wonderful thought indeed. At least it is interesting and worthy of profound consideration.
quotes.note: Note the register: “we believe that we have a mother there,” and then the doctrine is commended as “interesting and worthy of profound consideration” rather than taught as known. The quotation mark before “When you pray” is never closed in the vault text collated against the scan, and is preserved here rather than silently repaired. Spacing before semicolons and colons normalized; no words changed. The hymn was sung by the Tabernacle Choir that morning, which is how it entered the discourse — worship first, doctrine after.

quotes.excerpt: "I had learned to call thee Father, Through thy spirit from on high, But until the key of knowledge Was restored, I knew not why." "In the heavens are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare. Truth is reason. Truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there."
quotes.note: Punctuation follows the 1929 Conference Report printing, which differs from the hymnal text (commas for semicolons, a period after “stare”). See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: To say the least, if we are led to believe that we have a Father in heaven, I think we are justified in believing that we have a Mother there. Who ever heard of a father where there was no mother?
quotes.note: The Erastus Snow argument from nature, compressed to a single rhetorical question and shorn of the anatomy — and hedged twice over (“to say the least,” “I think we are justified in believing”). Sixty-two years later Gordon B. Hinckley will make the identical move in the identical words of logic: “Logic and reason would certainly suggest that if we have a Father in Heaven, we have a Mother in Heaven.” That the inference survives verbatim across the whole twentieth century, while the anatomical premise behind it disappears, is the point of filing this entry next to snow-heavenly-mother-1885 and hinckley-daughters-of-god-1991.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1929/1929-10-31-rudger-clawson-remarks-38.md, whose Final Review collated §0 against the archive.org scan conferencereport1929sa, leaves n105–n109, fixing OCR errors and a page-break sentence split. Provenance caveat worth carrying: the October 1929 ingest suffered the same systemic corruption as April 1929 — sequential “remarks-N” filenames with fabricated dates and session labels assigned by file position — and the heavyweight pass reconstructed the true date (October 6, 1929) and session from the report's own headers, so the filename is not evidence of anything. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. The vault frontmatter gives the generic “General Authority”; Clawson had presided over the Quorum of the Twelve since 1921. Filed as an original with the citesId edge preserved because the argument in q3 is Clawson's own and is not in the hymn. This entry and grant-o-my-father-1938 open the 1925–1965 stretch in which the hymn keeps circulating while almost no one argues from it.

title: Heber J. Grant reads “O My Father” into the conference record
speaker: Heber J. Grant
venue: General conference, opening address, first day morning session (Conference Report, October 1938)

quotes.excerpt: I have a little book in which I have recorded from time to time for many years items that have very profoundly impressed me… I have decided to read here today a part of what was in my Christmas greeting. I wish that all that is in my greeting might be read by all of the Latter-day Saints. As our conference proceedings are to be published, that is my excuse for reading a portion of this book entitled, "Treasures I Would Share," which was distributed by me for Christmas of 1937.
quotes.note: The mechanism of transmission, stated by the transmitter. Grant's reason for reading the hymn aloud is explicitly that the Conference Report will print it — he is using the opening address as a publishing channel. That is why this entry exists: nothing is argued, and the whole text of the hymn enters the official record anyway.

quotes.excerpt: I had learned to call thee Father, Through thy Spirit from on high; But until the Key of Knowledge Was restored, I knew not why. In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason, truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: The Mother stanza, read by the President of the Church in the opening address of general conference. Spacing before semicolons normalized from the printed OCR, and the hymn's verse line breaks are rendered as running text; no words changed. See o-my-father.

quotes.excerpt: When I leave this frail existence, When I lay this mortal by, Father, Mother, may I meet you In your royal courts on high? Then, at length, when I've completed All you sent me forth to do, With your mutual approbation, Let me come and dwell with you.
quotes.note: The closing stanza, which is where the hymn does its heaviest devotional work: the Mother is not merely posited, she is addressed, and reunion with her is the thing prayed for. This stanza, not the “parents single” couplet, is what most twentieth-century speakers actually quote — Henry D. Taylor in 1961, Hugh B. Brown in 1968, Neal A. Maxwell in 1978 — which is why phrase searches for “parents single” badly undercount the cluster.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1938/1938-10-heber-j-grant-selections-from-treasures-i-would-share.md, whose Final Review collated the text against the archive.org scan conferencereport1938sa, leaves n2–n16, with reading order rebuilt from the scan's DjVu word coordinates; five running-head bleeds were removed and side-heads converted to headings, no wording changed. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. A pure citation and deliberately so — Grant makes no argument about a Mother in heaven, offers no gloss, and does not pause at the stanza. He is reading ten favorite poems and hymns from a Christmas booklet, and “O My Father” is the fourth of the six he got through before the clock beat him. The entry earns its place on office and date rather than content: this is the President of the Church putting the full text of the doctrine's primary vehicle into the printed proceedings in 1938, in the middle of the stretch where the dataset otherwise goes quiet. Transmission without argument is the characteristic mid-century mode, and this is the cleanest specimen of it.

title: Joseph F. Merrill: half the couplet, and “leave mysteries alone”
speaker: Joseph F. Merrill
venue: General conference, Saturday evening session (Conference Report, October 1943, pp. 85–87)

quotes.excerpt: Well, yes, we are going to live a long, long time, and many of the things, that we would like to know, we will have an opportunity to learn, when we pass beyond this sphere, if we are willing to comply with the conditions for advancement… Yet we are taught that “as God now is, man may become.” How may man become like God? By working, advancing, growing, increasing, by his efforts, and he will have a long, long time in which he can continue those efforts.
quotes.note: The half-couplet. Merrill quotes only the forward line, “as God now is, man may become,” and never the backward one; this is the standard mid-century citation habit and it is why couplet counts overstate how often the Father's past mortality was actually preached. Note also what the forward line is made to mean here: post-mortal *learning*, not offspring, not worlds, not godhood. The register is self-improvement.

quotes.excerpt: Now as to precept, I believe it is extremely important to confine our teaching to fundamentals. On this matter may I say I am strongly influenced, have been influenced for a considerable number of years, by the attitude of the late President A. W. Ivins. When we teach by precept, he said, we should confine our attention to things that are fundamental and leave mysteries alone.
quotes.note: Context rather than an independent claim, and deliberately not tagged RETREAT-REFRAME: Merrill's counsel is a general instruction to Church educators, not a ruling on this doctrine, and tagging it would be retrojection. It is recorded because of where it sits — an apostle who spent years as Church Commissioner of Education, telling teachers in the same address to stay on fundamentals and then reaching for the safe half of the couplet. Merrill defines a mystery procedurally: any passage on which informed readers disagree.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1943/1943-10-merrill-by-precept-and-example.md, transcribed from the Church History Library preservation scan of the printed Conference Report (Internet Archive conferencereport1943sa, printed pp. 85–87, leaf n86) with reading order reconstructed from the DjVu word coordinates; the file is status published. Conference Report, so A. Chosen over Merrill's April 1945 conference address (conferencereport1945a), which carries the same half-couplet — “a characteristic teaching of the Church is that ‘as God now is man may become’ — a statement in poetic language of our magnificent doctrine of eternal progression” — in a single sentence and nothing else; the 1943 address gives the same formula plus the mysteries counsel and the post-mortal-learning gloss, so it is the stronger of the two. Merrill's April 1944 address (“Man Inherits Attributes of God His Father”) is a third witness to the same theme and contains the striking “we are of the race of the Gods,” but no couplet; it is left out to avoid three near-identical Merrill entries. Note the delivery setting: an off-the-air session, spoken extemporaneously, which is why the doctrine appears as an aside.

title: Stephen L Richards: eternal increase, mentioned “with a little hesitation”
speaker: Stephen L Richards
venue: General conference, first day morning session (Conference Report, April 1945)

quotes.excerpt: …held out for those who attain exaltation which I mention to you with a little hesitation because I have not yet laid the foundation for it, and that is this: That these eternal homes of the future life shall be blessed with eternal increase so that families never cease growing in number, in virtue and power…
quotes.note: Increase named, and glossed as families “growing in number” — one step past the bare word but still short of naming spirit children or a mechanism, so FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than FORWARD-EXPLICIT. The self-conscious framing is the datum: an apostle in general conference flags the doctrine as something he mentions “with a little hesitation,” and justifies raising it only because a later argument depends on it. Compare the confidence of talmage-af-1899 (“the Church proclaims the eternal truth”) forty-six years earlier.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1945/1945-04-stephen-l-richards-teachings-of-the-church-set-forth-in-a-letter.md, transcribed from the Internet Archive scan of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1945a, leaves 27–34) with reading order reconstructed from the DjVu XML. Conference Report, so A. The vault file is status draft and the surrounding paragraph carries two visible OCR artifacts (“p'romise”, “Creator of. the universe”); the excerpt is trimmed at both ends to a clean run and the elisions mark that trimming, not omitted argument — a maintainer should re-check this one against the page image before publication. The address is Richards reading and expounding a letter he had written setting out Church teachings for an enquirer, which is why the tone is expository. The passage stands two paragraphs after his statement that exaltation is “a never-ending experience in eternal progression and achievement,” and immediately before he tells the congregation that “much of this may seem highly theoretical and ethereal to you.”

title: Marion G. Romney: “I do not know the process”
speaker: Marion G. Romney
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1948)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, April 1948 (118th Annual Conference)
witnesses.note: Authoritative CHL catalog record, call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–, for the printed Conference Report. The vault treats this as canonical and the Internet Archive preservation scan conferencereport1948a as the page-by-page collation witness; the archive.org leaf anchor n76 is taken from the vault's own Final Review collation record.

quotes.excerpt: I believe he is the Father of my spirit and the Father of your spirit. I believe we were born to him and to our mother in heaven. I do not know the process, but I do know how we are born to our fathers and mothers in this earth and that is the way I think about it.
quotes.note: The most candid statement of the viviparous model in the twentieth-century pulpit corpus, precisely because it is offered as a personal working picture rather than as doctrine. Romney disclaims the mechanism in the same sentence in which he supplies it: the process is unknown, the earthly analogy is what he substitutes, and he says so. Tagged SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS as stated, not implied — he does state that this is how he conceives it — with the hedge preserved here rather than in the tag. Compare pratt-seer and ballard-increase, where the same picture is asserted as physiology.

quotes.excerpt: I believe I was born to him as a spirit child in the spirit world before I was born here, and what I say about myself — and you will pardon the personal reference — I feel about every other human soul that lives in the earth. I believe we all lived with him before we came here.
quotes.note: The generalization: the personal testimony is immediately extended to every human being, which converts an autobiographical belief into a universal claim about origin without ever changing register.

quotes.excerpt: I have here in this book a talk upon which I have spent many hours in thought and preparation. I had intended to give it at this conference… I shall therefore not talk on that subject, but I will ask each of you, if you will, to offer a silent prayer in your heart for me… that I may have the Spirit of the Lord while I speak to you wholly extemporaneously.
quotes.note: Provenance, and it is load-bearing. Romney abandoned his prepared text because President David O. McKay had just given the same talk, and delivered this one unwritten. The Heavenly Mother passage is therefore unrehearsed — which is exactly why it is valuable evidence of the ambient mid-century understanding, and exactly why it should not be pressed as a considered doctrinal formulation.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1948/1948-04-marion-g-romney-conference-address.md, whose Final Review collated the body against the independent scan OCR conferencereport1948a, leaves n76–n79, at 0.9839 similarity with no vault change needed; the sole flagged span proved to be a running-head artifact in the scan's raw reading order rather than a vault error. Conference Report, so A; historical-official — the Church's online conference archive begins in 1971, so no hosted page exists. No hymn quotation appears, hence no citesId. This is the strongest single find in the 1925–1965 stretch: an Assistant to the Twelve, speaking extemporaneously in general conference, states spirit birth from a Mother in heaven and simultaneously admits the mechanism is unknown to him. Distinct from the 1964 Romney entry already in the dataset (see romney-1964) and from eldred-smith-no-increase-1948, which was delivered at the same conference era and takes the opposite line on divine progression.

title: Milton R. Hunter: “he is a man — an exalted man”, with all knowledge
speaker: Milton R. Hunter
venue: General conference, first day morning session (Conference Report, October 1948, pp. 13–18)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, October 1948 (call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; the Church's own online conference archive does not reach back before 1971.

quotes.excerpt: We believe that God is a personal being. By a personal being, we mean that he is a man — an exalted man. Approximately one hundred years ago, soon after Lorenzo Snow became a member of the true Church of Jesus Christ, he formulated a remarkable couplet which has since that time become famous. He said: “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” (Lorenzo Snow, The Millennial Star 54:404.)
quotes.note: Both halves of the couplet, quoted in full, cited to a printed source, and used as the definition of what “personal being” means — not as an aside. “Exalted man” is attainment language, hence FATHER-BECAME-GOD; the couplet supplies the mortality, hence FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE as well. The referent is unambiguous because the whole address is about “God the Eternal Father… Elohim.”

quotes.excerpt: It is the first principle of the Gospel to know for a certainty the character of God, and to know that we may converse with him as one man converses with another, and that he was once a man like us; yea, that God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did. . . . … God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man, and sits enthroned in yonder heavens. That is the great secret.
quotes.note: Hunter reading the King Follett Discourse aloud in general conference in 1948, cited to Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, pp. 345–346 (see kfd-1844). Two paragraphs of Hunter's block quotation, with a third between them omitted at the … (“I will go back to the beginning before the world was, to show what kind of a being God is…”); the spaced full stops inside the first paragraph are the printed ellipsis of Hunter's own quotation, not an editorial cut. Worth registering as a fact about the period: the King Follett material was not merely surviving in books in the 1940s, it was being read from the pulpit at general conference.

quotes.excerpt: We believe that God is omniscient: that he is all-knowing, that he sees all things and that he hears all sounds. In other words, that his sight and his hearing know no bounds, and that his knowledge is absolutely unlimited.
quotes.note: Denial, sitting in the same address as the strongest backward claim of the mid-century conference corpus — the cleanest single-speaker demonstration in this window that the two axes are independent. Hunter holds that the Father was once a man and progressed to godhood, and that his knowledge is now absolutely unlimited. MANY-WORLDS is carried by the neighbouring sentence in the same section: “through his understanding of those laws and by putting them into operation he has created worlds without number, that is, they are not numbered to mortal man.”

quotes.excerpt: I know that we will some day return to the presence of God our Eternal Father and become exalted, glorified, and celestialized beings, receiving a portion, along with him, of the great glory that he possesses.
quotes.note: The forward half as Hunter closes it — “a portion” of the Father's glory, alongside him. Compare his April 1949 address six months later (hunter-beget-spirit-children-1949), where the same speaker names the generative content outright. The two together show how much the explicitness varies within one man's conference preaching.

title: Eldred G. Smith: in worlds without end shall have no increase
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1948)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, October 1948 (call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; the Church's own online conference archive does not reach back before 1971.

quotes.excerpt: Are you teaching your children to keep the Word of Wisdom only because it is a good health habit, or are you teaching them that by not keeping the Word of Wisdom they are not eligible to receive the knowledge and understanding to comprehend the laws of godliness, and so will be deprived of the opportunity to receive the power of the priesthood, and then not be permitted to enter the temple and thereby lose all the blessings of increase for all eternity? That is quite a price to pay, I would say. We are told they will become ministering angels, and in worlds without end shall have no increase. (See D. & C. 132:15-18.)
quotes.note: Eternal increase affirmed entirely by negation — the doctrine appears only as the thing the unworthy forfeit. Euphemism rather than explicit: “increase” is named and nothing else is, no offspring, no mechanism, no godhood. Note also the chain of consequence being drawn, from the Word of Wisdom through the temple to eternal increase, which is what puts a cosmological doctrine into a talk about parental teaching.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1948/1948-10-eldred-g-smith-conference-address.md, whose text was collated page-by-page against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1948sa, leaves n90–n93) at 0.983 similarity with no divergence beyond spacing and hyphenation. Conference Report, so A. The printed Report supplies no formal title; the vault's is supplied from the discourse headings. What this entry documents is a register shift rather than a new claim. By mid-century the generative doctrine is preached almost exclusively in this negative, temple-marriage-incentive form: not “you will bear spirit children” but “they shall have no increase.” D&C 132:17 is cited, the entailment is intact, and the content has become an argument for a behavior — which is how a doctrine can remain formally in force while ceasing to be described.

title: Milton R. Hunter: begetting spirit children “on the same principle”
speaker: Milton R. Hunter
office: Of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1949)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, April 1949 (119th Annual Conference)
witnesses.note: Authoritative CHL catalog record, call no. M205.1 C536 v. 1–69 1902–1970, for the printed Conference Report. The Internet Archive preservation scan conferencereport1949a is the collation witness; the leaf anchor n65 is taken from the vault's own Final Review collation record (leaves n65–n72, similarity 0.9793).

quotes.excerpt: they were all sons and daughters of God the Eternal Father and our Eternal Mother in that celestial spirit realm before we came into mortality. We are taught that we were born into that spirit realm as babies, and that we grew to maturity there, undergoing the various experiences which were there for us prior to our coming to mortality.
quotes.note: Not merely birth but infancy and maturation — spirits “born into that spirit realm as babies” who “grew to maturity there.” That is the viviparous model carried past the moment of birth into a full developmental biography, which is further than the nineteenth-century sources usually go and further than anything the Church teaches now. Presented as catechesis: “We are taught.”

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith explained that this continuation of "the seeds" forever and ever, meant the power of procreation; in other words, the power to beget spirit children on the same principle as we were born to our Heavenly Parents, God the Eternal Father and our Eternal Mother. Therefore, a man cannot receive the highest exaltation without a woman, his wife, nor can a woman be exalted without her husband.
quotes.note: FORWARD-EXPLICIT: not “eternal increase,” not “eternal family units,” but the power to beget spirit children, named. And the symmetry is stated rather than left to inference — the begetting exalted couples will do is “on the same principle” as the begetting that produced us, so the forward and backward directions are one mechanism. This is the D&C 132:19 “continuation of the seeds” reading (see dc-132) delivered plainly from a general conference pulpit in 1949. The gloss is credited to Joseph Smith; Hunter gives no citation for that attribution.

quotes.excerpt: Then shall they be gods. (Ibid. 132:19-20.)
quotes.note: Context for the two quotes above: Hunter has just read D&C 132:19–20 aloud, and the “continuation of the seeds” gloss is offered as exegesis of the verse he read. Untagged — the scriptural text is already in the dataset at dc-132; what is being catalogued here is Hunter's reading of it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1949/1949-04-milton-r-hunter-conference-address.md, whose Final Review collated §0 against conferencereport1949a, leaves n65–n72, at 0.9793 similarity with no body change required. Conference Report, so A; historical-official. No hymn quotation, hence no citesId. Hunter appears four times in the 1945–1949 conference corpus on this theme; this is the strongest and it supersedes the others — his October 1945 address (“Man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents… we are gods in embryo”) and his April and October 1949 remarks on Eternal Parents say less, in weaker language, than this one paragraph does. Together with romney-mother-in-heaven-1948 it shows that the mid-century quiet in the dataset is an artifact of collection, not of doctrine: the strong generative teaching was still being preached in general conference in the late 1940s, in the plainest available words, by a member of the First Council of the Seventy who was also the Church's most prolific popular theologian of the period.

title: Milton R. Hunter: “the power to beget spirit children,” and our Eternal Mother
speaker: Milton R. Hunter
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1949)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, April 1949 (call no. M205.1 C536 v. 1–69, 1902–1970)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; the Internet Archive item conferencereport1949a is the Church History Library preservation scan the vault text was collated against.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet Joseph Smith explained that this continuation of “the seeds” forever and ever, meant the power of procreation; in other words, the power to beget spirit children on the same principle as we were born to our Heavenly Parents, God the Eternal Father and our Eternal Mother. Therefore, a man cannot receive the highest exaltation without a woman, his wife, nor can a woman be exalted without her husband.
quotes.note: The whole package in two sentences, from the pulpit at general conference: increase glossed as procreation, the object named as spirit children, the mechanism named as “the same principle” by which we were born, and the Heavenly Mother named as a parent in the premortal birth. SPIRIT-BIRTH-VIVIPAROUS rather than adoption because the analogy Hunter draws is to birth, not to sealing. No backward claim about the Father's own origin is made, so the referent stays n/a: this is the forward direction only.

quotes.excerpt: …they shall pass by the angels and the gods, which are set there, to their exaltation and glory in all things, as hath been sealed upon their heads, which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods.
quotes.note: D&C 132:19–20 as Hunter reads it (see dc-132), including the bracketed insertion “[and if they commit no sin to break that seal]” earlier in the verse, which is his. The revelation supplies the euphemism — “a continuation of the seeds” — and the quote above is Hunter supplying the referent for it. This is the pairing the whole dataset turns on: the scripture is opaque, the exposition is not.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1949/1949-04-milton-r-hunter-conference-address.md, whose text was collated page-by-page against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1949a, leaves n65–n72); the file is status published. Smith's negative one (eldred-smith-no-increase-1948, eldred-smith-slavery-godhood-1950) are being preached from the same two verses in the same three-year stretch.

title: Eldred G. Smith: the difference between slavery and godhood for eternity
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
venue: General conference, second day morning session (Conference Report, April 1950)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, April 1950 (call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; collated against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1950a, leaves n66–n71).

quotes.excerpt: I tell others, many of them, the difference between civil marriage and celestial or temple marriage is the difference between slavery and godhood for eternity. The Lord makes it sound a little nicer when he says those who reject the law of celestial marriage will be ministering angels, and worlds without end shall have no increase. Waiting on others with no further progress is an eternal existence but is not real living. Living involves progress.
quotes.note: Godhood named, and named as the stake in a marriage decision. The remarkable clause is the second one: “The Lord makes it sound a little nicer” is a speaker telling a general conference audience, in as many words, that the scriptural language is a softening of what he has just said plainly. Still FORWARD-EUPHEMISM and not FORWARD-EXPLICIT on this dataset's precedent — no offspring, no mechanism, nothing but the word “increase” doing the work (compare dc-132, where “then shall they be gods” is graded the same way).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1950/1950-04-smith-i-hope-the-lord-will-bless-me.md, whose text was collated page-by-page against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1950a); the file is status published. title: Spencer W. Kimball: “eternal increase, perfection, and with it all — Godhood”
speaker: Spencer W. Kimball
venue: General conference, Friday morning session (Conference Report, April 1952)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, April 1952 (call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; collated against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1952a, leaves n20–n25).

quotes.excerpt: The blessings of eternity contemplated in this “all” bring to men immortality and everlasting life, eternal growth, divine leadership, eternal increase, perfection, and with it all — Godhood.
quotes.note: The closing sentence of the address, and a list rather than an argument: increase is one item in a series terminating in Godhood, with the dash doing the emphasis. The “all” is from the parable of the prodigal son, “all that I have is thine,” which Kimball has spent the previous paragraphs on.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1952/1952-04-kimball-i-pray-for-the-spirit-of-the.md, whose text was collated page-by-page against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1952a); the file is status published. title: Joseph Fielding Smith: “our Father had a Father and so on” — one page after “How God Does Not Progress”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Doctrines of Salvation, comp. Bruce R. McConkie (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1954), vol. 1, ch. 1 “Character, Attributes, and Perfections of God”

quotes.excerpt: It seems very strange to me that members of the Church will hold to the doctrine, “God increases in knowledge as time goes on.”… But, how does anyone know? Where has the Lord ever revealed to us that he is lacking in knowledge? That he is still learning new truth; discovering new laws that are unknown to him? I think this kind of doctrine is very dangerous. I don't know where the Lord has ever declared such a thing. It is not contained in any revelation that I have read.
quotes.note: Denial. The section heading standing over this text is “HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS,” and the paragraph heading is “FALSE NOTIONS ABOUT GOD'S PROGRESSION.” The unnamed “recently published article” he quotes and rejects is not identified in the book.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet says: “If Jesus Christ was the Son of God, and John discovered that God the Father of Jesus Christ had a Father, you may suppose that he had a Father also.” Then he asks: “Where was there ever a son without a father? And where was there ever a father without first being a son?”
quotes.note: Smith quoting the Sermon in the Grove — see sermon-grove-1844 — and quoting the second question as well as the first, which is the one that makes the series unbounded in both directions at once.

quotes.excerpt: Yet we have to pass through mortality and receive the resurrection and then go on to perfection just as our Father did before us. The Prophet taught that our Father had a Father and so on. Is not this a reasonable thought, especially when we remember that the promises are made to us that we may become like him?
quotes.note: “And so on” is the whole regress in three words, and it is offered as “a reasonable thought” rather than as a mystery to be handled carefully — from the same author, in the same chapter, who calls belief in God's progression in knowledge dangerous.

notes: Verified by re-pulling the whole of chapter 1 and reading the section sequence in order: THE GODHEAD, MODERN KNOWLEDGE OF GOD, HOW GOD PROGRESSES, HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS (with FALSE NOTIONS ABOUT GOD'S PROGRESSION, PERFECTION OF GOD NOT “RELATIVE,” SCRIPTURES PROVE OMNIPOTENCE OF GOD, GOD PROGRESSES BECAUSE OF KNOWLEDGE, WILL GOD DESTROY HIMSELF?), then HOW GOD IS EVERLASTING (with GOD IS AN EXALTED MAN and CHRIST BORN; YET FROM EVERLASTING), then HOW GOD IS FROM ETERNITY TO ETERNITY. The progression denial and the chain affirmation are separated by roughly a page of text and six intervening headings, so they are recorded here as separate quotes and must never be ellipsed together into one sentence, which is how the pair usually circulates. Taken together they are the cleanest single demonstration in this dataset that divine ancestry and divine progression are independent axes: Smith prints the chain approvingly a page after calling belief in God's continuing progression “very dangerous.” The chain half is expressly attributed to Joseph Smith and quotes both the Sermon in the Grove and the King Follett Discourse (see sermon-grove-1844 and kfd-1844). Graded never-official: Doctrines of Salvation is a Bookcraft compilation of Smith's sermons and writings assembled and captioned by Bruce R. McConkie, not a church publication, though it has long been treated as authoritative. The copy collated is a reflowed digital edition without the printed pagination, so sections are cited by heading; printed page numbers were not confirmed and are not asserted.

title: Hugh B. Brown reads Widtsoe on God's growth, then draws the line: “deify man,” not humanize God
speaker: Hugh B. Brown
office: Assistant to the Council of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, third day morning meeting (Conference Report, April 1956)

quotes.excerpt: In the beginning, which transcends our understanding, God undoubtedly exercised his will vigorously and thus gained great experience of the forces lying about him. As knowledge grew into greater knowledge by the persistent efforts of the will, his recognition of universal laws became greater until he obtained at last a conquest over the universe which to our finite understanding seems absolutely complete.
quotes.note: Brown reading John A. Widtsoe aloud in general conference (“On this point Dr. Widtsoe wrote as follows:”), from A Rational Theology — see widtsoe-rational-theology-1915. Every verb is completed: gained, grew, became, obtained at last. That makes it FATHER-BECAME-GOD, not DIVINE-PROGRESSION, on the same reading that separates talmage-conference-1915 from talmage-af-1899. Attainment language with no explicit mortality, so FATHER-BECAME-GOD alone. What Brown leaves out is the finding: Widtsoe's paragraph in A Rational Theology continues “if the great law of progression is accepted, God must have been engaged from the beginning, and must now be engaged in progressive development” — the present-tense clause, the one that actually asserts ongoing divine progression, does not survive into the 1956 pulpit relay. Two printed paragraphs are joined here with a space; nothing between them is omitted.

quotes.excerpt: If God is in fact our Father, then we, Father and children, belong to the same society of eternal intelligences. Among them he is supreme, he is the most advanced, most powerful, and most intelligent.
quotes.note: Context for the quote above and the one below, not tagged on its own. It is the ontology that makes the rest coherent — God and men as members of one society of co-eternal intelligences, differing by position on a scale — and it is argued from Abraham 3:19, 22, which Brown quotes immediately after. Naming God “the most advanced” of a class implies a scale he ascended, but Brown does not say so, and the no-retrojection rule keeps it out of the categories.

quotes.excerpt: When we say man may become like our Father, we do not mean to humanize God, but rather to deify man — not as he now is but as he may become. The difference between us is indescribably great, but it is one of degree rather than of kind.
quotes.note: The boundary drawn explicitly, in the sentence right after the Widtsoe reading: whatever the doctrine means, it does not mean bringing God down. The reframe and the claim are doing opposite work in the same breath — “degree rather than of kind” is the strong version of the teaching, and “we do not mean to humanize God” is the disclaimer attached to it. Compare packer-parentage-1984, where the same defensive move has hardened into a redefinition.

quotes.excerpt: To deny the possibility of eternal progression is to accept the awful alternative of eventual stagnation which would be damnation.
quotes.note: The stagnation argument, applied to man. B. H. Roberts had used the identical reasoning about God in 1911 — “an absolute immutability would require eternal immobility” (roberts-progress-of-god-1911) — and by 1956 it is being deployed for human progression only. Same argument, subject quietly changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1956/1956-04-brown-1-wonder-if-sometimes-our-people-think.md, transcribed from the Internet Archive scan of the printed Conference Report (conferencereport1956a, leaves n103–n106). Conference Report, so A. The vault file is status draft with an OCR-and-auto-clean provenance and no archive snapshot yet, and it records no calling; Brown was an Assistant to the Council of the Twelve in April 1956 (ordained an Apostle April 1958, First Presidency 1961), confirmed from the calling recorded on his other 1954–1956 conference files in the same corpus. title: Henry D. Taylor: the hymn's closing prayer, mid-century
speaker: Henry D. Taylor
office: Assistant to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles

quotes.excerpt: We sing a beautiful hymn that is a favorite of mine. It refers to our existence prior to coming to this earth. Sister Eliza R. Snow, the author, poses some very meaningful questions, and in addressing our Father in heaven asks:
quotes.note: The framing, and the reframing. This is the mid-century handling in miniature: the text is preserved intact and its most distinctive claim is quietly not the point.

quotes.note: The Mother addressed directly, in general conference, in 1961. Punctuation follows the Conference Report printing, which uses semicolons where the hymnal has commas. Taylor attributes the hymn by title. See o-my-father.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1961/1961-10-taylor-we-sing-a-beautiful-hymn-that-is.md, whose Final Review collated §0 against conferencereport1961sa, leaves n101–n103, removing two running-head bleeds mid-sentence and making no other body change; the heavyweight pass rebuilt the report's reading order from the scan's DjVu word coordinates and corrected the date and session from the report's own dateline.
